title: Is it too bad to use AI not only for coding, but for art, sounds and music?
author: Ok_Entertainment1608
selftext:
So, I use Claude to build a PC-building sim called PCValley. It has its own engine, uses its own scripting language called VaLang, and has a shit ton of languages (Norwegian, Russian, English, Estonian etc). And for all the month I have been building it the only question that has came up to me to the code is whether people would judge, hate or call my game slop just because I... Well, only tested it, because I do not know how to draw, make sounds, music, or code.  
Would you call a game bad because AI has been used for most of the things while the creator has actually tested the game?

comments.author: Aspiring_Serf
comments.body: Just do what makes you happy man.

comments.author: DeanRayGames
comments.body:
People who hate on generative AI generally give a pass to coding with AI. But music, art, etc, is anathema to them. No matter how good it is, no matter how good your final product is, if you did anything "artistic" with generative AI, they will hate your game, avoid it, or even review bomb it. 

Most people, however, just want to play a good game.

comments.author: M4xs0n
comments.body: Do whatever it takes to accomplish your vision

comments.author: OrderAmongChaos
comments.body: This depends too much on what the game looks like. Ask yourself: does my art feel like it's one project for my game, or does it feel like 100 submissions from random people? Does my music match the tone of my game or does it feel jagged and cobbled together? A game needs to feel like it has one cohesive vision, concept, art style, sound style and while it's possible to get that from an AI, it takes a lot of time and energy. If you let the AI make all the art and sound design decisions, you'll end up with a mess that everyone colloquially calls slop. In other words, you have to think of yourself as an art director. You don't need to actually perform the labor of making the art, but you need to know what you want and have to follow the general process of idea -> concept drawings -> style guides -> production.

If it wasn't constantly discussed, it wouldn't hurt for it to come up sometimes, but it's like every day, which is excessive for a space that is literally for AI enabled game development.

comments.author: municar
comments.body: most people will only care if it's good or not. there are a bunch of AI slop games on steam now that are just a front end for a spreadsheet with a really shiitty electron front-end that look and feel like a windows 3.11 app. you will need to get good enough at coding and UX design to be able to build those systems. you will probably be better served finding public domain or free for non-commercial use art assets than vibe-coding them, you generally need to be an artist to get good output from AI. or you could start using blender etc. yourself with AI to get better at those things. i would use ai-generated assets as placeholders and then spend the time finalizing them when you have the rest of the game nailed down

comments.author: Acid_Viking
comments.body: It's fine to use AI for art, sounds and music, as long as it's good. Human effort and creativity should be part of the process. You want art and music that you feel proud of, that reflects your vision. If the AI in your game looks/sounds like slop, people will assume that the gameplay, balance, etc., are also sloppy.

comments.author: h1soft
comments.body:
Honestly the thing players notice isn't "AI was used", it's when the pieces don't look like they belong to the same game. I ran into that on my mobile roguelike with environment art: tiles generated one at a time never matched each other. What fixed it was generating one big concept image and cutting it into wall blocks, ledges and backdrop strips, so everything comes from the same picture.

The other thing to watch: models make scenes way too busy. I kept having to pull detail out so the player and enemies stayed readable. If your stuff feels consistent and you've actually played it a lot, that's most of the battle.

comments.author: TrashWriter
comments.body:
Personally I won't play/buy a game that uses AI art or Music. But code is fine with me, being a software engineer (10yrs) and an artist (25yrs) I see both sides from both perspectives. 

Software is built on more communal (open source) and information sharing culture. Nobody cares if you copy and paste a snippet from stack overflow to fix your broken controller or method, in fact, good on you for finding an easier way to do something without spending a bunch of capacity. Nearly everything you do with coding, is built on documentation, stack overflow, and open source projects. The languages are literally built to have conventions in the way that you do things. 

In art, part of what makes art interesting is the process and the built up experience of the artist, I have one eye that is stronger(?) than the other, so without glasses my perspective is literally skewed (flat screens look like trapezoids) so the way that I draw has always been impacted by that. there are countless different minute details about the way that I personally do things that makes my art unique. and theres probably only a few other people on the planet alive today who do things the same exact way when it comes to art (if any at all). If you can't draw, that's fine. Cut someone into your project who can, or buy assets made by humans on the unity or unreal store or even booth.pm. Asset flips are infinitely more respectable in my eyes than AI generated assets. For the price of the AI plan that you would need for several months to produce anything even remotely respectable you could also buy assets. 

At the end of the day, do what you want, but if I can smell that AI smell when it comes to the assets, I won't be playing your game.
